passage: The maths olympiad was on Saturday, and on Friday evening Darshan was bouncing a football against the lift lobby wall of their Chennai apartment block. Madhav came down with his practice booklet. "Aren't you revising?" "Nah. I'm not even going to try this time." Darshan kicked the ball harder. "Olympiad is for toppers. If I don't study, it doesn't matter what I get." "But you got the top score in the class test." "That was easy stuff." Bounce. Bounce. Upstairs, his olympiad book sat under his bed, still in its plastic cover. On Monday, when the results came, Darshan got 38 out of 100. "I didn't even study," he announced loudly to the whole bench, before anyone had asked.

qa.q: Where was Darshan's olympiad book on Friday evening?
qa.a: It sat under his bed, still in its plastic cover.

qa.q: Why did Darshan announce 'I didn't even study' before anyone had asked?
qa.a: If the low mark came from not studying, nobody, including Darshan, has to think he isn't clever; the excuse protects how smart he feels.

qa.q: What small step on Friday could have helped Darshan face his fear?
qa.a: He could have revised just one chapter with Madhav, so trying felt smaller and the result would show what he really knew.

qa.q: How might Madhav see Darshan's 'I'm not even going to try'?
qa.a: Madhav remembers Darshan's top score in the class test, so the refusal may look puzzling, more like fear than laziness.

grounding: A boy skips revising for an exam he fears so a poor mark can be blamed on not trying.

passage:
'Harsha, your spelling test is tomorrow. Want me to quiz you?' Gargi didi held up the list.
'No.'
'Just ten words?'
'I said no. I'm not studying for it.' Harsha lay on the carpet, building a tower of dominoes.
'Why not? You love spelling.'
'Because.' A domino fell. 'If I don't study and I get a bad mark, it's only because I didn't study.'
'And if you do study and get a bad mark?'
Harsha's hands stopped. 'Then I'm just bad at spelling. Last time I studied and still got "necessary" wrong. Ma'am read my mark out.'
Gargi sat down on the carpet. 'That's a scary feeling. Want to practise only the hard ones with me? If some are still wrong, we'll know which to fix.'
Harsha looked at the list for a long moment. 'Only five.'

qa.q: Which word did Harsha get wrong last time?
qa.a: Harsha got "necessary" wrong, and Ma'am read the mark out.

qa.q: Why does not studying feel safer to Harsha?
qa.a: A bad mark after no studying can be blamed on not trying, while a bad mark after studying would feel like proof of being bad at spelling.

qa.q: What choice did Gargi offer, and why might it work?
qa.a: Practising only the hard words together keeps the effort small and turns wrong answers into a list to fix rather than a verdict.

qa.q: What is it like for Gargi to hear why Harsha won't study?
qa.a: Gargi learns the refusal comes from fear after last time, not laziness, so she sits down to help instead of scolding.

grounding: A child refuses to study for a feared spelling test so a bad mark won't mean being bad at spelling.

passage: I'm Nirmala, and this is about the science test in March. I was scared of it because Tenzin always gets full marks, and everyone thinks I'm the clever one too. The night before, I watched cartoons instead of opening my book. I told myself, "If I don't try, it doesn't count." In class the next day I told Tenzin, "I didn't even open the book," kind of proudly. I got 11 out of 25. I kept saying, "I didn't even study," so nobody would think I wasn't smart. But at home I felt weird inside, because I didn't actually know if I could have done better. Next time I want to try properly, even if it's scary, so I know.

subtype: Not studying so failure has an excuse [Actor]
passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 5B, Thursday. Jyoti Ma'am.
Before the English test, Ankita told the girls at her table, loudly, 'I didn't study at all. I watched cartoons the whole weekend.' She said it three times. Her hands were cold when I gave her the paper.
She scored 22 out of 40 and immediately said, 'See? Because I didn't even try.' She looked almost relieved.
Ankita is a bright reader. I think she is so scared a low mark means she isn't clever that not trying feels safer.
What I did: I spoke to her alone at lunch. I said a mark shows what to practise, not how clever someone is. We picked two things to work on. Next test, I'll ask what she practised.

qa.q: What did Ankita say she did all weekend?
qa.a: She said she watched cartoons the whole weekend.

qa.q: Why did Ankita look almost relieved after the low mark?
qa.a: Because she had said she didn't try, the 22 out of 40 didn't have to mean she wasn't clever; the excuse protected her from that fear.

qa.q: Which choice by Jyoti Ma'am could help Ankita try fully next time, and why?
qa.a: Talking to her alone, separating the mark from cleverness and picking two things to practise; asking what she practised makes effort the thing that counts.

qa.q: How might the girls at Ankita's table see her loud 'I didn't study at all'?
qa.a: They may think Ankita doesn't care about marks, without guessing at the cold hands and the fear underneath.

grounding: A teacher notes a child who announces she did not study before a test she fears, so a low mark cannot say she is not clever.

Harish
